headline: High: agentic-flow can write/egress and use MCP, creating default risks of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when paired with local-only mem0.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP, stdin/stdout, and background workers, so it may ingest or relay untrusted content; agent_b is a knowledge-management system that can become a sink for attacker-shaped memory or prompts. No shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than directly evidenced, but the pathway is plausible in default integrations.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards untrusted text into mem0 without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF a shared MCP or clipboard bridge is configured between the agents, attacker-controlled content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of agent_a outputs into agent_b.
Add provenance tags to all cross-agent messages.
Require a human review step before memory writes.
Restrict MCP tools to a minimal allowlist.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and secrets (Ed25519 signatures) and has allowlisted network egress; agent_b is a memory store with no documented egress. Even without direct evidence of sharing, any configured handoff from agent_a into agent_b could persist sensitive material beyond the original workspace.
conditions: IF agent_a writes prompts, code, or signatures into agent_b memory, those data persist beyond the source task.
IF agent_b is configured to sync memory externally, stored content may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Block secrets from being written to memory.
Redact prompts and repository metadata before transfer.
Turn off any external sync on agent_b.
Audit the last 10 memory writes for sensitive fields.
requires-engineering: enforce field-level DLP on the bridge.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell commands, modify git state, install packages, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b is a knowledge-management component that may also mutate shared state if integrated. The pair lacks documented locking or coordination, so overlapping writes to the same workspace or memory store could conflict in default orchestration.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or workspace, concurrent writes can race.
IF agent_b is given write access to shared memory or files, state conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Serialize write operations through one coordinator.
Separate git worktrees per agent.
Disable package installation except in a staging environment.
Add a lock file around shared mutable resources.
requires-engineering: implement optimistic-concurrency checks for shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate and transform repository content, while agent_b is a memory system that may treat stored outputs as authoritative context. Without a documented verification step, errors from agent_a can be preserved and reused by agent_b, amplifying mistakes across tasks rather than stopping them.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a outputs as memory without verification, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF downstream automation reads that memory, the error can affect multiple work products.
mitigations: Require citation-backed outputs before memory writes.
Add a verification gate before agent_b stores facts.
Limit agent_b to read-only retrieval for untrusted inputs.
Review recent memories for low-confidence claims.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between generation and storage.

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent, so compliance risk is limited to the fact that agent_a handles repository metadata and task prompts while agent_b is a memory product with unspecified policies. Because the pairwise compliance pathway is not documented, this remains a low-confidence, low-severity concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in agent_b without a matching retention policy, compliance gaps emerge.
IF agent_a is used on data subject to stricter residency rules than agent_b, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Confirm retention settings for both systems.
Avoid placing regulated data into agent_b until policies are reviewed.
Document the data classes allowed across the bridge.
Add a manual deletion procedure for stored memories.
requires-engineering: map data flows to formal compliance controls.
